Method

How PMS returns are measured, and how we rate

What the numbers on our PMS pages mean, the yardstick each strategy is held to, how the score is built, how often ratings change, and what the evidence does and does not show.

YardsticksThe scoreReview cycleEvidence
APMI data toOct 2026Ratings reviewed on data toOct 2026Next review: data to Dec 2026

Where the numbers come from

SEBI requires every portfolio manager to report each strategy ("investment approach") to APMI, the Association of Portfolio Managers in India, every month: client money at the month end and returns over 1, 3 and 6 months, 1 to 5 years and since launch. APMI publishes them. We read every month's report from April 2023, when the reports became complete, to Oct 2026.

What the returns mean

  • Time-weighted (TWRR): the return of the strategy itself, not affected by when clients added or took out money. Your own return differs with your timing.
  • After all fees and expenses, including any profit share, and before your tax. In a PMS you own the shares, so you pay capital gains tax on every sale the manager makes.
  • Periods over a year are annualised.
  • Discretionary strategies: the manager decides and trades for every client in the same model portfolio. In non-discretionary ones each client approves each trade, so the reported return depends on the clients' choices; we list them but do not rate them.

One yardstick per asset class

A strategy is only as good as what it is compared with. A small-cap manager who beat Nifty 500 during a small-cap rally showed no skill; a debt strategy compared with a share index tells you nothing. So each asset class has its own yardstick, read from the strategy's own returns (APMI gives no style labels):

  • Equity: the style index the strategy tracked most closely over its record (the lowest tracking error) among Nifty 50, Nifty 500, Nifty 500 Multicap 50:25:25, Nifty Midcap 150 and Nifty Smallcap 250 TRI. Strategies are then ranked within their style: large and multi cap, or mid and small cap.
  • Debt: the median high-quality bond mutual fund (corporate bond, banking and PSU, short duration) month by month: what the investor would otherwise hold.
  • Hybrid and multi-asset: the passive mix of Nifty 500 TRI and that bond yardstick that matched the strategy's ups and downs most closely, in 5% steps (for example 60% equity, 40% bonds). A strategy with more equity does not win just because shares rose.

The score

Each measure is turned into a percentile within the peer group (100 = top) and blended with the weights below. Rated: discretionary strategies with ₹100 crore or more (kept until they fall below ₹75 crore), a 3-year return and at least 24 months of monthly record.

Tiers

  • A+ Leading: top 10% of the peer group and a score of 70 or more.
  • A Strong: top 30% and 55 or more.
  • B In line: the middle.
  • C Lagging: bottom 30%.

A or A+ also needs a lead over the yardstick both over 3 years and over the whole record (positive alpha); otherwise B. A strategy whose clients withdrew more than 30% of its money in the last 12 months is held at B, with the reason shown.

How often ratings change

Returns, risk figures and money flows update every month, when APMI publishes (we load each month on the 20th). Ratings are reviewed quarterly, on data to March, June, September and December. At each review a strategy keeps its tier unless it has moved clearly past the boundary: 5 percentile points and 5 score points. In our test, re-rating every month would have changed the average strategy's tier about twice a year; quarterly with this buffer, about once every 16 months. Material events do not wait: the withdrawal rule and the ₹75 crore floor apply every month. The last review used data to Oct 2026; the next uses data to Dec 2026.

What the evidence says

We tested every measure on every discretionary equity strategy with ₹100 crore or more at each month-end from March 2025 to March 2026 (about 300 strategies each time, including ones that later shrank or closed), against the next 12 months' return over its index.

  • The measures we weight most (alpha, information ratio, share of months and of 12-month spells ahead) lined up with the next year at every one of the 13 test dates.
  • Last year's return, what most PMS rankings use, lined up least, and against Nifty 500 not at all.
  • Past volatility and worst falls lined up strongly with the next year's worst fall: risk persists, which is why the score keeps a risk pillar.
  • Strategies in the top 30% by our score went on to beat their index over the next 12 months 64% of the time, by a median of 2 points a year; the bottom 30% trailed slightly.

Honest limit: 13 overlapping test dates are about one and a half independent years in one market. This shows the measures are sensible; it does not show they forecast. Our ratings describe track records.

What it cannot tell you

  • APMI has 43 months of complete data: one long rise and one fall in Indian shares. Strategies that closed drop out of the reports.
  • No holdings, fees or style labels are in APMI's data. Credit strategies earn part of their lead over the high-quality bond yardstick by taking credit risk, which the risk measures only partly capture.
  • Your return differs from the strategy's with your timing and fee plan. Read the disclosure document, and judge a PMS over years.

Source: APMI (Association of Portfolio Managers in India) monthly reports, which portfolio managers file as SEBI requires. Returns are time-weighted, after all fees and expenses and before the investor's tax; periods over a year are annualised. Each strategy is compared with its own yardstick: equity with the style index it tracks most closely (total-return), debt with the median high-quality bond mutual fund, hybrid with its fitted mix of the two. Ratings describe past track records and are not a recommendation or a forecast; past performance does not guarantee future returns. PMS investments need at least ₹50 lakh, can lose value and carry higher fees than mutual funds; read the portfolio manager's disclosure document before investing.
